meta.title: Can I Poo in the Garden? — Wonderlab — The Wonderists
meta.description: On growing up without outgrowing wonder. Children ask an astonishing number of questions. Somewhere along the way, many of us learn to value answers more than questions. What happens if we don't?

article.title: Can I Poo in the Garden?
article.subtitle: On growing up without outgrowing wonder.
article.imageAlt: A woman in the wild, smiling toward the sun
bodyBefore: Children ask an astonishing number of questions. I’ve tried counting with my own daughters and usually lose track long before breakfast.
Can I poo in the garden?

Children seem remarkably comfortable being curious. They poke at the obvious and ask questions adults stopped noticing years ago. There’s so much they want to understand, and they don’t seem particularly concerned about looking knowledgeable while they’re at it. Although the garden question may have been less about understanding the world and more about negotiating the facilities.

Somewhere along the way, many of us begin valuing answers more than questions. The right answer earns a tick. “I’m not sure yet” can feel strangely uncomfortable. We learn that certain questions make people squirm, and that admitting we don’t know something can feel embarrassing. Bit by bit, we favour certainty over curiosity.

Curiosity leaves room to be surprised, to learn and unlearn. It asks, Why? What if? What am I missing? It moves towards discovery and gives us permission to change our minds when new evidence arrives.

And sometimes curiosity is a gap that wants to be closed. You notice something you don’t know and you go looking for an answer, most likely chatting with your AI. Sometimes that answer satisfies you. Sometimes it opens ten more questions.

Wonder can feel different. You don’t necessarily feel that anything is missing. Something in front of you is simply bigger than the frame you brought to it, and for a moment, you stop. The ridiculous vastness of the night sky. Your child asking where the wind sleeps. Curiosity might make you lean in; wonder can pin you to the spot. It doesn’t necessarily need an answer, and it doesn’t always arrive as a question. Sometimes it simply reminds you that the world is stranger, bigger and more extraordinary than you’d been paying attention to.
article.pullQuote: Curiosity might make you lean in; wonder can pin you to the spot.
bodyAfter: Learn how a rainbow works and you might satisfy your curiosity about its colours. It can still stop you in the driveway with your coffee going cold in your hand. Knowing how something happens doesn’t exhaust what’s extraordinary about it. Sometimes the explanation makes it even more remarkable.

And sometimes the two work together. A question draws you closer, and what you discover leaves you more astonished than before. You understand a little more and begin to sense how much there is still to discover.

Answers have never been easier to come by. You can ask an AI whether fish get thirsty and get an explanation in seconds. As AI takes on more of the answering, our ability to ask good questions becomes more valuable. What are we curious enough to investigate? What are we taking for granted? Have we understood the problem, or are we getting very efficient at solving the wrong one?

The questions we ask shape what happens next. “How can I get more done?” sends us in a different direction from “What’s actually worth doing?” “How do I convince them?” opens a different conversation from “What would make this irresistible to them?” A perfectly reasonable question can keep us circling familiar ground. A better one can open a door we hadn’t noticed.

Asking better questions takes practice. Pausing when something seems obvious. Following up with “Why?” Being willing to ask the slightly awkward thing everyone else appears to understand. Giving an answer enough attention to consider whether it makes sense, and what it leaves out.
article.closingStatement: We won’t always know where a question will take us. But in a world overflowing with answers, become the person who asks something worth thinking about.
